common_name: Dark Eyes Grape Hyacinth (Cobalt-Blue Muscari with White-Rimmed Tips)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep and 3-4 inches apart in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light shade; Dark Eyes bears unusually deep, saturated cobalt-blue florets edged in a crisp white rim.

directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep and 3-4 inches apart in fall in well-drained, average garden soil in full sun to light shade. Dark Eyes is distinguished from the standard grape hyacinth by flower spikes that read almost black-blue at the base of each urn-shaped floret, brightened by a thin, contrasting white rim at the mouth, giving the raceme unusual depth and contrast in mid-spring. It is otherwise as trouble-free as the species, multiplying steadily by offset bulbs and self-seeding to form larger drifts over the years, and pairs well with later-flowering pale tulips or daffodils once its deep color has had a season or two to spread. Allow the grassy foliage, which emerges the previous autumn, to yellow and die back naturally after bloom rather than cutting it back.

common_name: Ocean Magic Grape Hyacinth (Bicolor Dark-Blue-and-White Muscari)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep and 2-3 inches apart in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Ocean Magic opens dark blue at the base of the raceme and fades to icy white caps toward the top, like foam on a wave.

directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep and 2-3 inches apart in fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Ocean Magic is a selection of the early-blooming, compact Muscari aucheri, producing dense, conical racemes whose lower florets open a rich dark blue while the upper buds stay pale, icy white, creating a distinctive two-toned effect that is more pronounced than in the straight species. It flowers in early to mid spring, ahead of many other grape hyacinths, and is lightly fragrant, naturalizing modestly without the aggressive self-seeding habit of Muscari armeniacum. Grow it at the front of a border, in a rock garden, or massed under deciduous shrubs, and allow the narrow foliage to die back on its own after bloom.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep and 3-4 inches apart in fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Saffier's tightly closed, medium-blue buds never fully open or set seed, giving an unusually long-lasting conical spike.

directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep and 3-4 inches apart in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light shade. Saffier, an RHS Award of Garden Merit holder, is an unusual grape hyacinth whose violet-blue, green-tipped buds remain closed rather than flaring open into the typical urn shape, so the flower spike neither fades nor sets seed and instead holds its tidy, conical form for an exceptionally long bloom period in mid-spring. Because it does not self-seed, Saffier spreads only slowly by bulb offsets, making it a tidier, less rampant choice than the common species for borders, containers, or rock gardens where unchecked grape hyacinth seedlings can become a nuisance. Leave the strap-like foliage to die back naturally once flowering finishes.

common_name: Touch of Snow Grape Hyacinth (Tricolor Blue-to-White Muscari)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep and 3-4 inches apart in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Touch of Snow shades from deep blue at the base of the raceme through royal blue to icy white at the tips.

directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep and 3-4 inches apart in fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade. Touch of Snow produces a gradient flower spike, with the oldest, lowest florets opening a deep blue, the florets above shifting to a lighter royal blue, and the newest buds at the tip staying an icy white, giving each raceme a frosted, tricolor appearance that shifts further as the bloom ages. It flowers for several weeks in mid-spring, is lightly fragrant, and is as easy and drought-tolerant as other Armenian grape hyacinth selections once established. Use it in drifts under deciduous trees, in rock gardens, or massed at the front of a mixed spring bulb border, and let the foliage die back naturally after bloom.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep and 3-4 inches apart in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Atrocaerulea is a deeper, more intensely saturated blue selection than the typical wild-type Siberian squill.

directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep and 3-4 inches apart in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade. Atrocaerulea is grown for nodding, bell-shaped flowers in an exceptionally rich, dark cobalt blue, a more dramatic and saturated shade than the already vivid blue of the common Siberian squill, opening in very early spring often alongside the last snow. Like the species, it naturalizes readily under deciduous trees and in turf, tolerating deep shade once the tree canopy fills in for summer, and multiplies steadily by both offset bulbs and self-sown seed to build dense carpets over a few seasons. Allow the narrow, strappy foliage to yellow and die back completely before mowing over naturalized lawn plantings.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep and 3-4 inches apart in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Violet Beauty opens star-shaped flowers in mauve-violet with a paler center, rather than the typical blue-and-white of the species.

directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep and 3-4 inches apart in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade. Violet Beauty is a color break from the familiar blue-and-white glory-of-the-snow, bearing loose clusters of upward-facing, star-shaped flowers in a soft mauve-violet with a paler, almost white center, opening among the very earliest bulbs in late winter to early spring. It naturalizes readily under deciduous trees and in rock gardens, self-seeding and multiplying by offset bulbs to form expanding colonies, and combines well with crocus, snowdrops, and other blue or pink Chionodoxa and Scilla selections for a mixed very-early-spring display. Leave the narrow, paired leaves to die back naturally after bloom.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light shade; unlike modern Dutch hyacinths, each Roman hyacinth bulb sends up several loose, slender flower spikes instead of one dense one.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart in fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light shade. Roman hyacinth is an old, sparser-flowered strain of the species native to the South of France, producing two or three slender, loosely set flower spikes per bulb instead of the single dense, top-heavy spike bred into modern Dutch hyacinths, so the stems are far less prone to flopping and the plant is more willing to persist and naturalize in the garden over years. Flowers are typically white, pale blue, or soft pink and carry the same sweet hyacinth fragrance, opening slightly earlier in spring than standard hyacinth cultivars. It has long been favored for gentle forcing indoors in bowls of pebbles and water as well as for naturalizing in milder-winter gardens; where winters are cold, mulch after the ground freezes and otherwise treat it as you would any hardy hyacinth.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; in zone 9, pre-chill bulbs in the refrigerator (not freezer) for 6-8 weeks before planting in December-January, since hyacinths need cold they may not otherwise get in mild winters.

directions: Plant pre-chilled bulbs 5-7 inches apart in well-drained, fertile soil in partial to full sun. Dating to 1880, Distinction is one of the oldest hyacinth cultivars still in cultivation, bearing an unusual dark maroon, almost beet-root colored spike that stands out sharply against the pastel pinks and blues of most other hyacinths. Its flower spike and overall stature run noticeably smaller than modern hyacinth cultivars, a trait of its age that happens to make it especially well suited to gentle indoor forcing in bowls or glasses as well as to garden display. In warm-winter Gulf South gardens, treat pre-chilled bulbs as an annual display planted in December or January for February-March bloom, since hyacinth bulbs rarely rebuild the cold exposure needed for strong repeat flowering without a fresh chilling period each year.

directions: Plant pre-chilled bulbs 6-8 inches apart in well-drained, fertile soil in partial to full sun. Introduced in 1936, Hollyhock is a double-flowered heirloom hyacinth with small, densely packed, pug-faced florets in a vivid rose pink, carrying the same intensely sweet fragrance as single-flowered hyacinths but with a fuller, more textured spike. It is consistently the latest hyacinth to bloom in most collections, extending the fragrant hyacinth season by a week or more after other cultivars have finished. In warm-winter Gulf South gardens, treat pre-chilled bulbs as an annual display planted in December or January for February-March bloom, since hyacinth bulbs rarely rebuild the cold exposure needed for strong repeat flowering without a fresh chilling period each year.

common_name: General Kohler Hyacinth (Historic Double Lavender-Blue Hyacinth)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; in zone 9, pre-chill bulbs in the refrigerator (not freezer) for 6-8 weeks before planting in December-January, since hyacinths need cold they may not otherwise get in mild winters.

directions: Plant pre-chilled bulbs 6-8 inches apart in well-drained, fertile soil in partial to full sun. Dating to 1878, General Kohler is one of the rarest surviving double hyacinths, its spike built of opulent, ruffled lavender-blue bells with a texture that has been likened to sculpted sugar frosting, carrying the same powerful, sweet fragrance typical of the species. Double hyacinths like this one were once the most prized form in the Dutch bulb trade before fashion shifted toward the simpler single-flowered types that dominate the market today, and only a handful of named doubles like General Kohler have survived in cultivation. In warm-winter Gulf South gardens, treat pre-chilled bulbs as an annual display planted in December or January for February-March bloom, since hyacinth bulbs rarely rebuild the cold exposure needed for strong repeat flowering without a fresh chilling period each year.

common_name: Chestnut Flower Hyacinth (Historic Double Dawn-Pink Hyacinth)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; in zone 9, pre-chill bulbs in the refrigerator (not freezer) for 6-8 weeks before planting in December-January, since hyacinths need cold they may not otherwise get in mild winters.

directions: Plant pre-chilled bulbs 6-8 inches apart in well-drained, fertile soil in partial to full sun. Introduced in 1880, Chestnut Flower is a double hyacinth with starry, overstuffed florets in a soft dawn pink, one of only a few named double hyacinths to have survived from the heyday of double-flowered forms in the nineteenth-century Dutch bulb trade. Its fuller, more textured spike carries the same intensely sweet fragrance as single hyacinths and makes an interesting contrast planted alongside modern single cultivars. In warm-winter Gulf South gardens, treat pre-chilled bulbs as an annual display planted in December or January for February-March bloom, since hyacinth bulbs rarely rebuild the cold exposure needed for strong repeat flowering without a fresh chilling period each year.

directions: Plant pre-chilled bulbs 6-8 inches apart in well-drained, fertile soil in partial to full sun, giving it at least a few hours of direct sun daily for the best flower color and sturdiest stems. Splendid Cornelia bears a dense spike of starry florets in an unusual pastel blend of lilac and mauve touched with blue, each floret further enriched with darker blue veining, carried on an atypical burgundy-tinted flower stem rather than the usual green. Highly fragrant and considered one of the better hyacinth cultivars for indoor forcing, it brings a softer, more refined color than the bold primary blues, pinks, and reds of most widely sold hyacinths. In warm-winter Gulf South gardens, treat pre-chilled bulbs as an annual display planted in December or January for February-March bloom, since hyacinth bulbs rarely rebuild the cold exposure needed for strong repeat flowering without a fresh chilling period each year.
